summary: Defines a service for locating Public Key Infrastructure repositories using DNS SRV records, per RFC 2782. This lets systems that use certificates find where certificates are kept. It is an experimental protocol.

plainLanguage.summary: A way to ask the internet's phone book where a certificate library is kept.

subtitle: How a certificate-using program can find a domain's PKI repository by asking DNS for an SRV record.

tldr.problem: Several RFCs define protocols for fetching certificates and revocation information from PKI repositories, but they assume the client already knows where the repository is and which protocol to use.
tldr.mechanism: A client queries DNS for an SRV record named _PKIXREP plus a protocol label (such as _LDAP, _HTTP or _OCSP) under the domain, and reads the host and port from the answer.
tldr.outcome: It gives clients that only have a domain name a common way to find repositories. The RFC is Experimental and is updated by RFC 8553.

today: RFC 4386 is an Experimental RFC and is updated by RFC 8553. It has not been obsoleted.

sections.title: Finding a PKI Repository
sections.content:
A PKI repository holds public-key certificates and revocation information. RFCs such as RFC 2559, RFC 2560 and RFC 2585 specify protocols for retrieving this data, but they assume the certificate-using system already knows how to identify, locate and connect to the repository with a given protocol.

Some protocol-specific tools exist, such as knowledge references in directory systems, but each works with a single protocol and there is no common way to publish them. This RFC fills the gap with DNS Service (SRV) resource records, defined in RFC 2782. It is expected to be most useful where only a domain name is available. If a certificate already holds the needed information, no DNS lookup is needed.
sections.plainLanguage: Programs know how to borrow certificates from a certificate library, but not where the library is. This memo says to look it up in the internet's phone book, DNS.

sections.title: The PKIXREP SRV Record
sections.content:
An SRV record has DNS type code 33 and the form _Service._Proto.Name TTL Class SRV Priority Weight Port Target. For this service the symbolic name is PKIXREP, and when used in an SRV record it MUST be prefixed with an underscore, giving _PKIXREP.

The protocol part of the name says which repository protocol the client wants. The RFC lists three: LDAP (_LDAP), HTTP (_HTTP) and OCSP (_OCSP).

New protocols are not added here. Their prefixes SHOULD be defined in the document that specifies the protocol.
sections.plainLanguage: The DNS entry has a name that says what you are looking for (a certificate library) and how you want to talk to it (LDAP, HTTP or OCSP). The answer tells you which computer and door to use.

sections.title: Querying and Multiple Repositories
sections.content:
A domain may offer several repositories that speak different protocols. The RFC says the client MAY discover them by making a separate DNS query for each protocol the client supports.

The RFC acknowledges this could become inefficient if repository protocols proliferate, and says the discovery protocol could then be extended so a repository could advertise the protocols it supports. That extension is only a possibility, not part of the RFC.

If the domain runs the service on several hosts, more than one SRV record is returned, and RFC 2782 defines how to decide which to try first.
sections.plainLanguage: If you can speak three languages, you ask the phone book once for each. If it lists several addresses, the phone book's usual rules tell you which to try first.

sections.title: Worked Example: Email Encryption
sections.content:
The RFC's example uses the fictional domain example.com. Alice's email client needs a certificate for the recipient, Bob, whose address is bob@example.com. Alice's client supports LDAP. Bob's certificate is in the domain's "border directory" repository at border.example.com.

The client queries DNS with QNAME _PKIXREP._LDAP.example.com, QCLASS IN and QTYPE SRV. The result SHOULD include the host address of the domain's border directory system, and the client can then fetch Bob's certificate over LDAP.
sections.plainLanguage: Alice wants Bob's certificate. She asks DNS where example.com keeps its certificates for LDAP, gets back the computer's name, and goes there to pick it up.

sections.title: Security and IANA Considerations
sections.content:
Security of the repositories themselves is out of scope. For LDAP repositories, security considerations are in RFC 2559. Security issues of SRV records in general are covered in RFC 2782 and apply here too.

IANA reserves the _PKIXREP service label and created a new registry, PKIX SRV Protocol Labels. An entry is a label name and a pointer to a specification describing how that protocol uses SRV, and specifications should meet the "specification required" policy of RFC 2434.
sections.plainLanguage: This memo does not make the certificate libraries themselves safe; other documents do that. IANA keeps a list of the allowed protocol names.
